case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s supervised-release term continues to run—and thus counts as “served”—during a period when the defendant has absconded from supervision, or instead is tolled (paused) until the defendant is back under supervision.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (especially § 3583(a) governing supervised release and § 3583(i) governing the court’s power to revoke after expiration), and related supervised-release timing/tolling provisions discussed by the parties (including references to 18 U.S.C. § 3624).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico argues she is entitled to credit for time that elapsed while she was a fugitive because the supervised-release “clock” runs unless Congress expressly tolls it; the statute does not contain an absconding-based tolling rule, and importing a judge-made “fugitive tolling” doctrine creates an extra-statutory, hard-to-define standard (‘abscondment’) that determines when a federal sentence ends. She contends it is conceptually inconsistent to say she was not serving supervised release (so no credit) while simultaneously saying she violated supervised-release conditions during that same period. She also emphasizes statutory structure: Congress provided a specific, limited post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i), which would be undermined if absconding automatically tolls the term and effectively prevents expiration. Finally, petitioner and amici stress administrability and due process concerns: courts differ on what counts as absconding and when it begins, and those indeterminacies should not control sentence length without clear statutory authorization.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that supervised release is fundamentally a period of supervision, so a fugitive is not meaningfully serving the supervised-release sentence; allowing the term to run while a defendant evades supervision would reward flight and permit defendants to ‘run out the clock,’ potentially avoiding revocation consequences for serious violations committed while absconding (including new drug crimes). The government supports a fugitive-tolling approach analogous to the longstanding rule that prison sentences are tolled by escape—one must actually be in custody to serve custody time, and similarly one must be under supervision to serve supervised release. It also argues that petitioner’s interpretation would produce perverse incentives and is inconsistent with supervised-release purposes and with the court’s ability to consider post-violation conduct when deciding revocation and sentencing outcomes.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (9th Cir. precedent referenced in district court colloquy)
Esteras v. United States (referenced in oral argument as a ‘last term’ decision on revocation factors)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that an absconder is not “meaningfully serving” supervised release—has intuitive force, but it still asks us to create an atextual stop-clock rule that effectively enlarges the sentence’s duration without a statutory trigger. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress specified tolling in § 3624(e) and separately provided a narrow, condition-laden post-expiration mechanism in § 3583(i); reading absconding tolling from silence would substantially dilute § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons requirement and upset that carefully drawn structure. Justice Gorsuch’s distinction from Mont matters to me: Mont was anchored in explicit tolling language Congress enacted, whereas here the Government seeks a general “no credit when supervision is frustrated” principle untethered from the text. Given Bowles’s caution (as Justice Sotomayor notes) against judicially crafting temporal extensions, the narrower, institutionally legitimate course is to hold the clock runs absent express statutory tolling, leaving any absconding-specific rule to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that an absconder is not “serv[ing] a term of supervised release” in any ordinary sense, so the term should not run; but that functional intuition cannot override the statute’s enacted timing mechanisms. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress expressly provided tolling in § 3624(e) and separately created a limited post-expiration revocation power in § 3583(i) conditioned on a timely warrant or summons—so an implied absconding-tolling doctrine would largely nullify § 3583(i)’s trigger and extend punishment beyond what the text authorizes. Mont does not help the government because it interpreted the specific tolling predicate Congress wrote; it does not license courts to invent additional stop-clock rules from silence. Bowles, as Justice Sotomayor notes, reinforces the separation-of-powers problem with judicially enlarging congressionally set temporal limits, whatever the policy concern about “running out the clock.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s negative-implication argument from § 3624(e) is the most serious textual objection, and I agree it narrows what we can responsibly infer from silence. But I remain persuaded that this case is not about creating an extra-statutory “tolling” category so much as applying the ordinary meaning of “serv[ing] a term of supervised release”: a defendant who deliberately absconds is not undergoing supervision at all, so the supervised-release component of the sentence is not being executed in any meaningful sense. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Bowles does not undermine that point, because Bowles involved a fixed, congressionally specified filing deadline, whereas here the question is whether time can count toward completion of a sentence component when the defendant has made that component impossible to administer. Finally, although Justice Kagan is right that § 3583(i) is a backstop keyed to warrants/summons, reading it to require the clock to run even during proven, intentional absconding would create perverse incentives and frustrate Congress’s supervision-centered design without any clear textual command to award credit for evasion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that an intentional absconder is not “meaningfully serving” supervised release, so the calendar alone should not confer credit; but that functional reframing still does the statutory work of tolling without an enacted tolling trigger and would, in practice, let courts extend a term beyond its stated end. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress built a timing architecture with express tolling in § 3624(e) and a carefully conditioned, warrant/summons-gated post-expiration revocation power in § 3583(i); an absconding stop-clock rule would substantially dilute § 3583(i)’s limits and invite uneven, factbound application. Mont does not undermine that conclusion because, as Justice Thomas notes, it construed Congress’s explicit tolling text rather than authorizing courts to create new tolling categories from silence. And Bowles supports restraint here: where Congress specified the conditions for extending authority past an endpoint, we should not manufacture an additional exception, even if it would address “run out the clock” incentives the government can mitigate through timely process.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the ordinary-language intuition that a person who willfully absconds is not really “serv[ing]” supervised release, so the clock should not run. But that functional premise can’t justify adding a stop-clock rule Congress did not enact, especially given the statute’s timing architecture: § 3624(e) contains an express tolling rule and § 3583(i) provides a carefully conditioned post-expiration revocation mechanism keyed to a warrant or summons. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice now emphasize, recognizing an atextual absconding tolling doctrine would substantially dilute § 3583(i)’s trigger and extend punishment beyond the term Congress authorized; Mont cuts the other way because it interpreted enacted tolling language rather than announcing a free-floating principle. The government’s “run out the clock” concern is real, but the workable textual solution is diligence plus § 3583(i), not a new judicially crafted tolling category.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that an absconder is not “serving” supervised release in ordinary terms, so the sentence component is not being executed and the clock should not run. But that functional framing still smuggles in a stop-clock rule the text does not supply, and it cannot be reconciled with Congress’s timing architecture: express tolling in § 3624(e) and the carefully limited post-expiration authority in § 3583(i) keyed to a timely warrant or summons, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize. Mont does not help the government because it interpreted an explicit tolling predicate Congress enacted; here, the requested tolling arises from silence, and Bowles’s warning against judicially enlarging congressionally specified temporal limits reinforces our institutional duty to leave that choice to Congress. I am persuaded as well by the Chief Justice’s revised view that the negative implication is dispositive and that § 3583(i) supplies the government’s remedy—diligence and timely process—without judicial invention.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the functional claim that a willful absconder is not “meaningfully serving” supervised release, so the term should not run. But as the Chief Justice now recognizes, Congress already built a timing architecture: express tolling in § 3624(e) plus the carefully limited post-expiration jurisdiction in § 3583(i) triggered by a timely warrant or summons, and reading an additional absconding-based stop-clock rule from silence would substantially dilute § 3583(i) and extend punishment beyond the term Congress authorized. Mont does not supply a free-floating principle to pause supervision whenever it is frustrated; it interpreted specific tolling text Congress enacted, which makes this case closer to Bowles’s institutional warning against judicially creating timing exceptions than to a mere “non-execution” concept. Practical concerns about “running out the clock” are real, but under my institutionalist, precedent- and text-respecting approach, they are better handled through diligent use of § 3583(i) or legislative change, not an atextual doctrine.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the ordinary-language intuition that someone who willfully absconds is not really “serv[ing] a term of supervised release,” so the clock should not run. But that functional premise cannot override the statutory architecture Congress enacted: § 3624(e) contains an express tolling rule, and § 3583(i) supplies a carefully conditioned, warrant/summons-based mechanism for post-expiration revocation—so adding an absconding toll from silence would largely displace § 3583(i)’s limits, as Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan stress. Mont does not supply a free-floating “non-service” principle; it construed the specific tolling text Congress wrote (“imprisoned in connection with a conviction”), which underscores the negative implication here. Bowles reinforces the institutional point (as Justice Sotomayor notes): we should not extend temporal limits on punishment by judicial invention when Congress has provided the relevant timing triggers and backstops.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the common-sense claim that a willful absconder is not truly “serving” supervised release, so the term should not accrue by mere passage of time. But that reframing still produces the legal effect Congress specifically regulated—extending the sentence’s end date—and, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress already built a timing architecture with one express tolling rule in § 3624(e) and a carefully conditioned post-expiration revocation pathway in § 3583(i). Unlike Mont, which interpreted explicit tolling text tied to imprisonment “in connection with a conviction,” the government here asks us to supply a new tolling category from silence, which risks bypassing § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons requirement and creating uneven, factbound extensions inconsistent with Bowles’s caution against judge-made temporal exceptions. The policy worry about “running out the clock” is real, but the statute’s practical remedy is diligence and timely process under § 3583(i), not an atextual stop-clock doctrine.

John Roberts.reasoning: Supervised release, by design, is a period of actual postconfinement supervision and monitoring, and a defendant who absconds is not meaningfully “serving” that term during the period she has placed herself beyond supervision. Consistent with Mont v. United States, 587 U.S. 514 (2019), the better reading of the statutory scheme is functional rather than purely chronological: time does not count as “served” when the defendant is unavailable for supervision, avoiding the perverse incentive to “run out the clock.” Section 3583(i)’s limited post-expiration revocation authority does not foreclose tolling, because it addresses the court’s retained power after a term would otherwise expire, not whether the term continues to run while supervision is being actively thwarted. A narrow holding recognizing tolling only during periods of willful absconding best fits the statute’s supervised-release purposes while preserving institutional legitimacy by aligning with Mont’s approach to “runs”/tolling questions under §§ 3583 and 3624.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 sets a supervised-release term as part of the sentence and provides an express, limited mechanism for post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) conditioned on issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration; courts should not graft an extra-textual “fugitive tolling” rule that effectively prevents expiration whenever a judge later deems conduct to be “absconding.” Congress knows how to toll time when it wishes, and § 3583 contains no absconding-based tolling provision, making the government’s approach an impermissible atextual modification of a jurisdictional boundary set by statute. Under a strict textualist approach, policy arguments about “running out the clock” cannot override the enacted limits, and administrability concerns reinforce that sentence length should not turn on a nebulous, judge-made standard. Bowles v. Russell underscores that courts may not create equitable exceptions to congressionally prescribed time limits, and § 3583(i) likewise should be enforced as written.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Textually, § 3583(a) makes supervised release a component of the sentence designed to be a period of actual supervision, and it is hard to say a defendant is “serving” that part of the sentence while intentionally beyond the reach of the probation office. Reading the statute to allow the term to run during abscondment would create serious practical consequences—rewarding flight and allowing defendants to “run out the clock,” thereby undermining revocation for serious violations—an outcome Congress is unlikely to have intended in a supervision-centric regime. Section 3583(i) is best read as a narrow backstop for late-initiated revocation proceedings after an otherwise-expired term; it does not require treating time as “served” when the defendant has made supervision impossible, and tolling in that circumstance does not contradict § 3583(i)’s limited post-expiration jurisdiction. The traditional analogy to escape from custody—one does not earn credit while frustrating execution of the sentence—supports tolling here, and nothing in the text compels a contrary, defendant-favoring rule that would impair law-enforcement and probation functions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3624(e) supplies Congress’s express tolling rule for supervised release (when the person is imprisoned on a new conviction), and its specificity strongly suggests courts may not add an extra, judge-made “absconding” tolling exception; under United States v. Johnson, when Congress provides exceptions, courts should not create others. Section 3583(i) also reflects Congress’s carefully limited post-expiration revocation jurisdiction, and adopting fugitive tolling would effectively expand that jurisdiction beyond what Congress authorized, contrary to the Court’s insistence in Bowles v. Russell that timing/jurisdictional rules must come from Congress rather than equity. The government’s policy concerns about “running out the clock” are real, but they are properly addressed through the statutory tools Congress provided (timely warrants/summons under § 3583(i), revocation and resentencing authority) rather than an indeterminate “abscondment” doctrine that risks unequal application and due-process problems. Given supervised release’s impact on liberty, especially for vulnerable defendants, I would not lengthen federal sentences absent clear statutory authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3583 sets a supervised-release term as part of the sentence, and Congress provided specific, text-based timing rules: tolling for imprisonment in § 3624(e) and a limited post-expiration revocation power conditioned on a timely warrant or summons in § 3583(i). Reading an atextual “fugitive tolling” doctrine into statutory silence would let courts extend supervision beyond the term Congress authorized (potentially beyond statutory maxima) and would largely circumvent § 3583(i)’s carefully drawn limits, raising serious administrability problems given the absence of any statutory definition of “absconding.” Bowles v. Russell underscores that when Congress and the Rules set sentence- or jurisdiction-adjacent time limits, courts should not create equitable add-ons based on general maxims like “no one benefits from his own wrong.” The government’s policy concerns are real, but Congress addressed them through § 3583(i)’s warrant mechanism rather than an indefinite, judge-made pause in the supervised-release clock.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text and structure of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 supply no absconding-based tolling rule, and when Congress wants supervised-release time not to count it says so expressly (cf. § 3624(e)’s explicit tolling in specified circumstances), so courts should not invent an extra-statutory “fugitive tolling” doctrine. Section 3583(i) provides a carefully delimited mechanism for post-expiration revocation jurisdiction; treating absconding as automatically stopping the clock would effectively expand that jurisdiction beyond the statute’s terms, raising separation-of-powers concerns. Whatever the policy appeal of preventing a defendant from “running out the clock,” that judgment is for Congress, and any ambiguity about sentence duration should be resolved against enlarging punishment under the rule of lenity. Bowles v. Russell’s insistence that courts may not create judge-made exceptions to congressionally set temporal limits reinforces that conclusion here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3583 does not expressly toll supervised release for absconding, and Congress’s supervised-release timing scheme instead relies on specific, express mechanisms—most notably § 3624(e) (tolling during imprisonment) and § 3583(i) (limited post-expiration revocation jurisdiction upon a timely warrant or summons). Inferring a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would effectively rewrite § 3583(i)’s limits and make sentence length turn on an indeterminate, extra-statutory concept of “abscondment,” raising serious administrability and legitimacy concerns. The government’s escape analogy has intuitive appeal, but unlike custody, supervised release is a statutory creature whose start/stop rules Congress has delineated in text, and this Court has cautioned against judicially creating tolling or jurisdictional extensions beyond what Congress provided. Consistent with Bowles v. Russell’s insistence that courts respect statutory limits rather than craft equitable exceptions, the supervised-release “clock” continues to run absent explicit statutory tolling, with § 3583(i) providing the backstop for timely-initiated revocation proceedings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The statutory text points against judge-made fugitive tolling: 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) specifies a single tolling rule (imprisonment in connection with a conviction) and says nothing about absconding, and under the negative-implication principle courts generally may not add exceptions Congress chose not to include. Section 3583(i) then supplies a limited, express mechanism for post-expiration revocation jurisdiction when a warrant or summons issues before expiration; implying automatic tolling for absconders would substantially diminish § 3583(i)’s role and alter the statute’s timing architecture. Consistent with Jama v. ICE, we should be especially reluctant to infer an unstated requirement where Congress has demonstrated in the same statutory scheme that it knows how to speak to timing and exceptions. Policy concerns about rewarding flight are substantial, but they cannot supply an atextual tolling rule that determines when a federal sentence ends.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3583 sets the supervised-release term as part of the sentence, and Congress specified a narrow tolling rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (imprisonment for another conviction) plus a limited post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i); that structure strongly suggests courts should not add an extra-statutory “absconding” tolling doctrine that effectively extends sentence duration. Creating a judge-made tolling rule here raises serious administrability and procedural-fairness concerns because “abscondment” lacks a statutory definition and would make the end date of a federal sentence turn on vague, factbound determinations without clear notice. Consistent with this Court’s strict approach to statutory time limits and separation-of-powers concerns in Bowles v. Russell, equitable or policy-driven tolling is not appropriate where Congress has spoken in adjacent provisions and omitted the asserted tolling ground. The government’s incentive arguments can be addressed through enforcement during the term and through § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism rather than by judicially rewriting the supervised-release clock.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether time on supervised release continues to run—and must be credited to the defendant—during periods when the defendant is a fugitive/absconding from supervision, or instead is tolled (paused) until the defendant is back under supervision.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (especially § 3583(i) regarding delayed revocation and the broader supervised-release scheme); related statutory context includes 18 U.S.C. § 3624 (release and supervision administration) as discussed in argument.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico argues that supervised release is a sentence whose term runs according to statute and the judgment, and Congress did not authorize courts to stop (toll) the clock merely because a person absconded. She contends that importing a judge-made 'fugitive tolling' doctrine into § 3583 is textually unsupported, hard to administer (because 'absconding' has no statutory definition and is fuzzy at the margins), and in tension with Congress’s specific mechanisms for handling violations—most importantly revocation proceedings and § 3583(i)’s limited extension of revocation authority after a term would otherwise expire. She also points out an internal logic problem in the government’s approach: the government seeks to treat her as bound by (and capable of violating) supervised-release conditions during the abscondment period while simultaneously claiming she was not ‘serving’ supervised release for purposes of credit. Under her view, violations committed while she was a fugitive can still be punished through authorized revocation tools—so long as the statute’s timing limits are satisfied—but the court cannot retroactively extend the supervised-release term by tolling it.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that allowing supervised-release time to accrue while a defendant is a fugitive would let defendants profit from evasion, undermining the central purpose of supervised release—actual monitoring and contact with probation. It maintains that, as a functional matter, a person who absconds is not serving the supervised-release component of the sentence (analogizing to the traditional rule that prison sentences do not run while an escapee is at large), and therefore should not receive 'credit' for time spent outside supervision. On this view, tolling is necessary to preserve courts’ ability to enforce supervision and address serious post-abscondment violations (e.g., new drug crimes) without defendants claiming the term expired while they were fugitives.
key_precedents: Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007) (raised in the lower court discussion as a jurisdiction/timing case, argued to be inapposite to supervised release)
Pepper v. United States, 562 U.S. 476 (2011) (cited in the resentencing context for considering post-offense rehabilitation)
United States v. Watson (9th Cir.) (Ninth Circuit precedent referenced in the district court colloquy as binding on fugitive tolling questions)
Esteras (Supreme Court, last term) (referenced in oral argument regarding supervised-release revocation factors and relevance of post-term conduct)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is the equitable intuition Justice Alito pressed—an absconder is not being supervised and should not be able to “run out the clock.” But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress already addressed post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) and conditioned that continuing authority on a warrant or summons issued before expiration; a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would largely bypass that calibrated trigger and convert a rule-like limit into an open-ended standard. Justice Thomas’s negative-implication argument from § 3624(e) reinforces the minimal, text-bound conclusion: when Congress wanted tolling, it said so, and its silence here is hard to treat as inadvertent in a criminal sentencing scheme. Under our institutional role, the policy concern is properly met by timely process under § 3583(e)/(i), not by judicially extending supervision beyond the term Congress authorized.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed as a fairness and “not meaningfully serving supervision” argument—cannot overcome the enacted text in a detailed sentencing statute. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress supplied an express, limited post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i) keyed to a timely warrant or summons; a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would effectively expand that authority and nullify Congress’s chosen trigger. The negative implication is reinforced by my comparison to § 3624(e): Congress expressly tolls supervised-release time for imprisonment, demonstrating it knew how to toll and chose not to do so for absconding. Whatever the equitable appeal of a “no profit from flight” principle, under an originalist and textualist methodology we may not extend restraints on liberty without clear statutory authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that § 3583(i) is Congress’s express, warrant-or-summons-triggered mechanism for post-expiration revocation, and that fact substantially weakens any judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine that would operate as an additional end-run around the statutory trigger. Justice Thomas’s negative-implication point from § 3624(e) is also significant: Congress demonstrated it knows how to toll supervised-release time and did so expressly in one context, making its silence here hard to treat as accidental in a criminal-sentencing scheme. The strongest contrary argument is the practical one I have pressed—an absconder is not meaningfully serving “supervised” release—but under a restrained textualism, that policy concern cannot justify extending a liberty-restricting term beyond what Congress authorized, especially where (i) already supplies a calibrated tool the government can use by timely seeking a warrant. Mont, as Justice Gorsuch notes, further cautions against making these timing rules malleable, and the absence of statutory definitions for when “absconding” begins and ends confirms that any broader fix is for Congress, not us.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains Justice Alito’s intuition that supervised release is “supervision,” so an absconder is not truly serving it and should not benefit from flight. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress already addressed post-expiration enforcement in § 3583(i) with a specific, warrant-or-summons-triggered mechanism; layering an atextual fugitive-tolling rule on top would effectively bypass that calibrated prerequisite and make the end of a criminal sentence turn on an undefined, fact-bound notion of “absconding.” Justice Thomas’s negative-implication argument from § 3624(e) further supports restraint: when Congress wanted tolling, it said so, and in this liberty-restricting context we should not extend supervision without clear statutory authorization. The policy concern is real, but it is for Congress (or for the government to act timely under § 3583(i)), not for us to create a vague tolling doctrine with foreseeable notice and disparate-impact problems.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point (pressed by Justice Alito) is that an absconder is not actually being supervised and shouldn’t be able to “run out the clock,” but that policy intuition cannot supply tolling authority Congress did not enact in a detailed sentencing scheme. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3583(i) is Congress’s express, calibrated answer for post-expiration revocation—and it turns on a warrant or summons issued before expiration—so a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would largely bypass that prerequisite and effectively convert a rule into an open-ended standard. Justice Thomas’s negative-implication point from § 3624(e) remains telling: Congress knew how to toll supervised-release time and did so expressly in one setting, making its silence on absconding hard to treat as inadvertent. The administrability and notice problems of defining when “absconding” starts and ends further counsel against judicial invention in a criminal context where end-dates should be determinate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed most forcefully by Justice Alito—is that an absconder is not meaningfully “serving” supervised release and should not be allowed to run out the clock by flight. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress already supplied a specific, rule-like solution for post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i), conditioned on a timely warrant or summons; adopting fugitive tolling would evade that prerequisite and effectively rewrite a calibrated limit into an open-ended, judge-made standard. Justice Thomas’s negative-implication argument from § 3624(e) remains decisive: Congress expressly provided tolling in one circumstance and a narrow continuation mechanism in another, so we should not invent additional tolling in a criminal sentencing scheme without textual authorization. Whatever the policy appeal, separation of powers and fair notice concerns counsel adhering to the statutory design and leaving any broader tolling rule to Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed most forcefully in Justice Alito’s earlier framing—is that an absconder is not meaningfully “serving” supervised release and should not be able to run out the clock, but that equitable intuition cannot supply tolling authority in a detailed sentencing statute. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress already calibrated the post-expiration revocation power in § 3583(i) and conditioned it on a timely warrant or summons; a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would largely evade that prerequisite and convert a rule-like limit into an amorphous standard. Justice Thomas’s comparison to § 3624(e) reinforces the negative implication: Congress knew how to toll supervised-release time and did so expressly in one context, so we should not infer an additional, atextual tolling regime here. Administrability and legitimacy concerns also cut against respondent—without statutory definitions for when absconding begins/ends, sentence end-dates would become uncertain in a way Congress’s scheme appears designed to avoid.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point (as Justice Alito frames it) is that absconding means the defendant is not truly “serving” supervised release, so the clock should not run. But the statutory text treats supervised release as a “term” imposed by the judgment, and Congress specified the only timing adjustments it wished to allow: express tolling in § 3624(e) and the narrowly conditioned post-expiration revocation authority in § 3583(i). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, those provisions carry a strong negative implication against a judicially created fugitive-tolling doctrine that would effectively bypass § 3583(i)’s warrant-or-summons prerequisite and turn a rule-like end date into an atextual, fact-bound “absconding” standard. The practical concern about fugitives “profiting” is addressed by Congress’s chosen mechanism—timely warrants and revocation—so I do not see a textual or precedential basis to extend supervision beyond the term Congress authorized.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—pressed most forcefully by Justice Alito—is that supervised release should involve actual supervision and an absconder should not be able to “run out the clock.” But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, Congress squarely confronted the post-expiration problem in § 3583(i) and conditioned continued authority on a timely warrant or summons; adopting a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would bypass that calibrated trigger and effectively extend liberty restraints beyond the term Congress authorized. Justice Thomas’s negative-implication point from § 3624(e) matters to me as well: Congress expressly provided tolling in one supervised-release timing context, which makes the omission here hard to treat as inadvertent in a criminal-sentencing statute where notice and administrability are paramount. Given the undefined boundaries of “absconding” and the procedural-fairness stakes, the better course is to require the government to use the statutory tools Congress supplied, rather than judicially inventing a tolling rule.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3583 sets out a detailed supervised-release scheme, including Congress’s targeted provision in § 3583(i) extending revocation authority after expiration only when a warrant or summons issues; that specificity counsels against grafting a broader, judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that effectively lengthens the term without statutory text. The government’s reliance on an escapee-sentence background principle is a substantial policy argument, but our cases caution against extending background tolling doctrines into materially different statutory contexts absent a clear indication Congress legislated against that backdrop (cf. Arellano and related equitable-tolling limits), and supervised release—unlike custody—turns on legal obligations and judicially imposed conditions rather than physical confinement. A narrow, institutionally legitimate resolution is to hold that the supervised-release term continues to run as imposed, while emphasizing that violations can be addressed through the mechanisms Congress provided—revocation under § 3583(e) and delayed revocation under § 3583(i) when its prerequisites are met—rather than by implied tolling that creates administrability problems and risks upsetting settled sentencing finality. This approach hews most closely to the statutory text, avoids creating an open-ended “absconding” standard by judicial invention, and respects Congress’s calibrated timing rules for revocation proceedings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not authorize judge-made “fugitive tolling,” and § 3583(i) instead supplies a limited, express mechanism for delayed revocation after a term would otherwise expire—suggesting Congress chose when (and only when) courts may reach beyond the term’s end. Congress also knew how to write an explicit tolling rule and did so in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (tolling during imprisonment for another conviction), so its omission of comparable language for absconding must be respected under ordinary textualist inferences. Reliance on policy concerns about defendants “profiting” from flight cannot overcome the statutory scheme Congress enacted, particularly where revocation authority exists but is constrained by the statute’s timing limits. To the extent the Government invokes common-law escape principles, any such background rule cannot supply tolling authority where Congress legislated a detailed supervised-release code without including it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme in 18 U.S.C. § 3583 is designed to ensure actual postcustody supervision; when a defendant absconds and places herself beyond supervision, she is not meaningfully “serving” that term, so the period should not be credited—otherwise defendants could profit from evasion and frustrate law enforcement’s ability to monitor and protect the public. Although § 3583(i) provides a limited delayed-revocation mechanism, it is best read as a backstop for timely-initiated revocation proceedings, not as an affirmative command that the clock must run even while the defendant is a fugitive, especially where such a reading would create perverse practical consequences. The Court’s discussion in Esteras confirms that post-term conduct can be highly relevant to revocation decisions, and it would be anomalous to treat serious conduct committed during fugitive status as “off the table” simply because the defendant successfully hid until the nominal expiration date. Petitioner’s reliance on Bowles v. Russell is misplaced because tolling here is not a judge-made exception to a congressionally jurisdictional deadline; it is a sensible interpretation of when the supervised-release term is being served within the statutory supervised-release framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme in 18 U.S.C. § 3583 sets out a detailed timing and remedial structure, and the only express tolling rule Congress enacted is in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (tolling while imprisoned for another conviction), which counsels strongly against courts creating an additional, atextual “fugitive tolling” doctrine. Section 3583(i) further confirms Congress chose a limited mechanism to preserve revocation authority after the term’s scheduled expiration—only if a warrant or summons issues before expiration—so judicial tolling would effectively circumvent those intentional constraints and expand punitive authority beyond what the statute authorizes. As this Court explained in United States v. Johnson, when Congress provides specific exceptions in a supervised-release statute, courts should not infer authority to create others, particularly where doing so risks administrability problems and disparate impacts on defendants with unstable housing or limited access to counsel. The Government’s fairness concerns about “profiting” from absconding can be addressed through the statute’s existing tools (timely warrants, revocation under § 3583(e), and appropriate revocation imprisonment), without retroactively extending the supervision term by judge-made tolling.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3583 sets a supervised-release “term” that runs from release, and Congress specified the only express mechanisms for stopping or extending the court’s revocation power—most notably § 3583(i), which preserves authority after the term expires only if a warrant or summons issues before expiration and the adjudication occurs within a reasonable time. Importing a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would effectively expand § 3583(i)’s carefully drawn limits and make the end-date of a sentence turn on an undefined, administratively fuzzy concept of “absconding,” with no textual anchor. The government’s policy concern that defendants should not profit from flight is substantial, but Congress addressed that problem through revocation and additional imprisonment under § 3583(e)(3), rather than by retroactively extending the supervised-release term. Given the statutory structure and the weakness of any inference from congressional silence, this is not a setting to create an extra-statutory tolling doctrine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3583 sets supervised-release terms by statute and judgment, and it nowhere authorizes a court to pause that term based on a judicially crafted “fugitive tolling” rule; where Congress wanted post-expiration authority, it spoke expressly and narrowly in § 3583(i), conditioning delayed revocation on a warrant or summons issued before expiration. Allowing tolling by implication would effectively rewrite § 3583(i)’s limited extension mechanism and create an extra-statutory exception to a time limit many courts (and this Court in Mont v. United States, 587 U.S. 514, 525 n.1 (2019)) have treated as jurisdictional, contrary to this Court’s insistence that equitable tolling cannot alter jurisdictional rules absent clear congressional authorization. Even if tolling sometimes operates as a background equitable principle, this Court’s tolling jurisprudence (e.g., United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, 575 U.S. 402 (2015)) requires a statutory basis to infer such modifications, and the absence of any statutory definition of “absconding” underscores the administrability and notice problems of making term expiration turn on a nebulous, judge-made standard. Any policy concern that absconders might “profit” is for Congress to address, and lingering ambiguity in this criminal sentencing scheme should be resolved under the rule of lenity rather than expanding judicial power to extend supervision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme in 18 U.S.C. § 3583 reflects Congress’s choice to specify when supervision may extend beyond its nominal end, and § 3583(i) provides a targeted, express mechanism for delayed revocation after expiration when a warrant or summons issues before the term ends—suggesting by negative implication that courts lack free-floating authority to toll the term based on judge-made “fugitive tolling.” The government’s proposed tolling rule has no clear textual anchor in § 3583, risks undermining administrability and workability given the statute’s lack of any definition of “absconding,” and invites courts to extend criminal punishment outside the limits Congress set, contrary to principles of judicial restraint. Whatever the intuitive appeal of preventing defendants from “benefiting” from flight, Congress addressed enforcement through warrants, revocation, and the limited post-expiration jurisdiction in § 3583(i), and we should not add an extra-statutory tolling doctrine. Consistent with institutional legitimacy and precedent-focused restraint, the better course is to apply the statute as written and leave any broader tolling rule to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme in 18 U.S.C. § 3583 provides specific mechanisms for addressing violations, and Congress expressly addressed the post-expiration problem in § 3583(i) by extending revocation authority only when a warrant or summons issues before expiration and the matter is resolved within a reasonable time—text that strongly counsels against an extra-textual fugitive-tolling overlay (expressio unius/negative-implication). Nothing in § 3583’s text authorizes courts to pause the running of the term based on a nebulous, nonstatutory “absconding” standard, and adding such a doctrine would undermine the administrable, rule-like limits Congress chose in § 3583(i). While the Government’s policy concern is substantial, this Court has been reluctant to create equitable exceptions that alter congressionally specified timing rules, see Bowles v. Russell, and Congress left courts ample tools through revocation under § 3583(e) and the limited delayed-revocation authority in § 3583(i).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3583 sets a supervised-release term that runs as part of the sentence, and Congress specified only limited circumstances for extending revocation authority after expiration in § 3583(i); importing a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would effectively rewrite that carefully bounded timing scheme. Unlike prison or parole custody in Anderson v. Corall, 263 U.S. 193 (1923), supervised release is a statutory, condition-based regime, and Congress’s omission of any tolling rule—despite addressing related timing/administration issues in § 3624—counsels against creating one judicially. The government’s policy concern that defendants “profit” from absconding is addressed through Congress’s chosen tools—revocation and reimprisonment under § 3583(e), including the ability to impose additional supervision—without the administrability and fairness problems of defining “absconding” and retroactively extending the term. Procedural fairness and predictable end-dates matter in a supervision system that carries significant liberty constraints, and § 3583(i) indicates Congress meant expiration to have real limiting effect absent timely warrants or summonses.
